items.title: Speed limit: max in ideal conditions
items.simple: The speed limit is the fastest you may drive. It is for perfect conditions. You may go slower if you do not hold up traffic. Going faster is against the law.
items.official: A speed limit is the maximum legal speed you can travel on a road under ideal conditions. You may drive slower than the speed limit, as long as you don't impede the normal movement of traffic, but it is illegal to drive any faster.
items.mnemonic: The limit is a ceiling, not a target.

items.title: Must slow for zones and weather
items.simple: By law, you must slow down when a school zone or work zone speed limit is in effect. You must also slow down when road work or bad weather makes the posted speed unsafe.
items.official: By law you must drive slower where signs indicate a school zone speed limit or work zone speed limit is in effect, and/or if conditions such as road construction or bad weather make the posted speed unsafe.

items.title: Reckless: 20+ over or 85+
items.simple: If you drive 20 MPH or more over the speed limit, police can charge you with reckless driving. They can also charge you if you drive over 85 MPH, no matter what the limit is.
items.official: If you are driving 20 or more miles per hour (MPH) above the speed limit, or over 85 MPH, a law enforcement officer may charge you with reckless driving, regardless of the speed limit.

items.title: Reckless driving is a crime
items.simple: Reckless driving is a crime called a misdemeanor. A judge can fine you, take away your license, or put you in jail. If reckless driving causes a death while your license is suspended or revoked, it may be a felony.
items.official: It is considered a misdemeanor criminal offense if convicted of reckless driving. The court may require a fine, suspend your driving privilege and/or impose a jail sentence. If the violation results in death and the operator's license was suspended or revoked at the time of the offense, it may be considered a felony.

items.title: Extra $100: 81-85 in 65
items.simple: Picture a 65 MPH zone. Driving 81 to 85 MPH there costs an extra $100 fine. You pay it if you are found guilty.
items.official: You are subject to an additional $100 fine if convicted of driving between 81 and 85 MPH in a 65-MPH zone.

items.title: Radar detectors are illegal
items.simple: You may not use a radar detector in Virginia. It is against the law.
items.official: It is illegal to use radar detectors in Virginia.

items.title: 25 MPH: school, business, homes
items.simple: If there is no speed limit sign, the top speed in school, business and home areas is 25 MPH.
items.official: Unless there is a speed limit sign stating otherwise, the maximum speed limit for passenger vehicles and motorcycles is 25 MPH for school, business and residential areas.

items.title: 35 MPH: unpaved roads
items.simple: If there is no speed limit sign, the top speed on an unpaved road is 35 MPH.
items.official: Unless there is a speed limit sign stating otherwise, the maximum speed limit for passenger vehicles and motorcycles is 35 MPH for unpaved roads.

items.title: 55 MPH: all other roads
items.simple: If there is no speed limit sign, the top speed on all other roads is 55 MPH. Other roads are all roads except unpaved roads and roads in school, business or home areas.
items.official: Unless there is a speed limit sign stating otherwise, the maximum speed limit for passenger vehicles and motorcycles is 55 MPH for all other roads.

items.title: School zones may use speed cameras
items.simple: Some school zones use cameras to catch speeders. A sign that says SPEED PHOTO ENFORCED tells you cameras check your speed there.
items.official: Some school zones may have automated photo enforcement, as indicated by signs with the message "Speed Photo Enforced" or similar.

items.title: Three parts of stopping distance
items.simple: Three things add up to your stopping distance. They are perception time, reaction distance and braking distance. Perception time is how long it takes you to spot a danger.
items.official: Three factors determine the distance that it takes to stop your vehicle: perception time, reaction distance and braking distance. Perception time: The time it takes you to recognize a hazard.
items.mnemonic: See it, react, brake: three parts of every stop.

items.title: Reaction distance
items.simple: You spot a problem. Then your foot moves to the brake. The distance your car travels in between is called reaction distance.
items.official: Reaction distance: The distance your vehicle travels between the time you recognize a problem and the time you apply the brakes.
items.mnemonic: Reaction distance: before the brake. Braking distance: after.

items.title: Braking distance
items.simple: Braking distance is how far your car moves after you press the brake. It gets longer when you drive faster, when your brakes or tires are worn, or when the pavement is bad.
items.official: Braking distance: The distance your car travels after you apply the brakes. Braking distance is also affected by how fast your vehicle is traveling, the condition of your brakes and tires, and the pavement condition.
items.mnemonic: Braking distance starts when your foot hits the brake.

items.title: What changes your stopping distance
items.simple: Your stopping distance changes with the weather, how well you can see, and how you feel. It also changes with your speed, the road conditions, how alert you are and your car's weight.
items.official: Perception time, reaction distance and braking distance are affected by weather, visibility, and your mental and physical condition. Road conditions, speed, driver alertness, and the weight of the vehicle you are driving all change the ability to stop.

items.title: Wet pavement doubles braking
items.simple: Wet pavement can double your braking distance. In the rain, you may need twice as much distance to stop.
items.official: Braking distance is also affected by ... the pavement condition. For example, wet pavement can double your braking distance.

items.title: Never pump antilock brakes
items.simple: Never pump antilock brakes. Learn how your brakes work. Read your owner's manual and practice braking before you drive on the road.
items.official: If your vehicle has antilock brakes, be sure that you understand how they work. Check your vehicle owner's manual and practice braking before you go out on the road. Remember, never pump antilock brakes.

items.title: Keep a space cushion
items.simple: Keep space all around your car. The space gives you room to react and avoid a crash. Stay in the middle of your lane. Leave room ahead of your car and behind it.
items.official: Space around your vehicle gives you distance to react in emergencies and avoid a crash. Create a space cushion around your vehicle by staying in the middle of your lane. Make sure there is enough room ahead of your vehicle and behind it for other vehicles to pass or stop safely.

items.title: Under 35 MPH: 2 seconds
items.simple: If you drive under 35 MPH on a dry road, stay at least 2 seconds behind the car ahead.
items.official: Following Distance: 2 seconds Under 35 MPH. At these speeds and on dry surfaces, this distance, in seconds, allows the driver to steer and brake out of a problem area.

items.title: 35-45 MPH: 3 seconds
items.simple: If you drive 35 to 45 MPH on a dry road, stay at least 3 seconds behind the car ahead.
items.official: Following Distance: 3 seconds 35-45 MPH. At these speeds and on dry surfaces, this distance, in seconds, allows the driver to steer and brake out of a problem area.

items.title: 46-70 MPH: 4 seconds
items.simple: If you drive 46 to 70 MPH on a dry road, stay at least 4 seconds behind the car ahead. If you speed over 70 MPH, these following distances do not work.
items.official: Following Distance: 4 seconds 46-70 MPH. The space cushions above do not work if you're speeding over 70.

items.title: Count seconds from a fixed mark
items.simple: Watch the car ahead pass a fixed object, like a sign or overpass. Count the seconds until you reach it. If you get there too soon, you are too close. Slow down.
items.official: Glance at the vehicle ahead as it passes a fixed object, such as an overpass, sign, fence, corner or other fixed mark. Begin counting the seconds it takes you to reach the same place in the road. If you reach the mark before you have counted off two, three, or four seconds, depending on speed, you're following too closely. Slow down and increase your following distance.

items.title: Add seconds when conditions are bad
items.simple: Add extra seconds to your following distance in bad weather or heavy traffic. Also add extra seconds on poor pavement or when your car is in poor condition.
items.official: For bad weather conditions, heavy traffic, poor pavement or if your vehicle is in poor condition, add extra seconds to increase your following distance. Drivers need to change following distance when speed or road conditions change.

items.title: Hand 1/2 second, foot 3/4
items.simple: Your hands react in about half a second. Your foot reacts in about three-quarters of a second. If you are tired, taking medicine or distracted, you react even more slowly.
items.official: Hand response time is close to a half second. Foot response time is normally three-quarters of a second. This does not take into account any delay in perception time as a result of the driver being tired, on medication, distracted, etc.
items.mnemonic: Hand and Half both start with H. Foot is slower: 3/4.

items.title: When to leave extra space
items.simple: Leave extra space behind a big vehicle that blocks your view. Leave extra space behind a motorcycle or bike. Also add space in bad weather, in heavy traffic, when you leave an expressway, and when someone is tailgating you.
items.official: Increase your following distance when driving: behind a large vehicle that blocks your vision; in bad weather or heavy traffic; when exiting an expressway; behind a motorcycle or bicycle; when being tailgated.

items.title: Being tailgated: no sudden braking
items.simple: A tailgater follows you too closely. Do not slam on your brakes. If you can, move to another lane. You can also tap your brakes gently and slow down. Then the tailgater can pass or back off.
items.official: Tailgating is when one driver follows another too closely. If you find yourself in this situation, do not brake suddenly. If possible, move over to another lane, or gently tap your brakes to flash your brake lights and slow down. This should encourage the tailgater to pass you or slow down. Help the driver behind you by maintaining a safe following distance and a steady speed. Tap your brakes to warn the driver behind you when you plan to slow down or stop.

items.title: Look 20-30 seconds ahead
items.simple: Look far down the road, 20 to 30 seconds ahead of your car. In the city, that is about one block. Keep your eyes moving. Do not stare at one thing or at the middle of the road.
items.official: Searching means looking at the entire scene for anything that might come into your path. As you search the road, avoid staring at one thing. Expert drivers try to focus their eyes 20 to 30 seconds ahead. In the city, that equals approximately one block. Avoid staring at the middle of the road. Scan from side to side.
items.mnemonic: 20 to 30 seconds ahead = about one city block.

items.title: Look left, right, left
items.simple: Before you enter an intersection, look left, then right, then left again. Look left first because cars from the left are closer to you.
items.official: Check from left to right and then left again before entering an intersection. At any intersection, look to the left first, since cars coming from the left will be closer to you. Then look to the right and take one more quick look to the left before you drive through.
items.mnemonic: Left is closest, so left is first and last.

items.title: Look both ways where paths cross
items.simple: Look both ways anywhere cars, people or animals may cross your path. Such places include intersections, crosswalks, shopping centers, work areas and playgrounds.
items.official: Whenever you reach a place in the road where other cars, people or animals may cross your path, look both ways to be sure it is clear. These include intersections, crosswalks, shopping centers, construction areas and playgrounds.

items.title: Check mirror every 10 seconds
items.simple: Check your rearview mirror often, about every 10 seconds. It shows if someone is coming up too fast or tailgating you. Also check it before you change lanes, back up or slow down quickly.
items.official: Use your rearview mirror to check the traffic behind you frequently, about every 10 seconds. This will alert you if someone is moving up too quickly or tailgating you. Check the traffic behind you when changing lanes, backing up, slowing down quickly or driving down a long, steep hill.

items.title: Clues a car may pull out
items.simple: Watch for clues that a car may pull into your path. Look for exhaust smoke, brake or back-up lights, and turned wheels. In the country, watch for hidden driveways, curves, hills and slow farm vehicles.
items.official: Search for clues on the road. Look for exhaust smoke, brake or back-up lights and turned wheels on vehicles. Clues like these warn that the vehicles may pull into your path. When driving in rural areas, watch for hidden intersections and driveways, curves, hills and different road conditions.
items.mnemonic: Smoke, lights, wheels: that car may move.

questions.explain: A 25 MPH limit applies in school, business, and residential areas unless a sign says otherwise.

questions.prompt: Unless a sign says otherwise, what is the maximum speed limit on unpaved roads?
questions.explain: The default speed limit on unpaved roads is 35 MPH.

questions.prompt: Unless a sign says otherwise, where does a 35 MPH speed limit apply?
questions.explain: Unpaved roads have a 35 MPH limit unless a sign says otherwise.

questions.prompt: Unless a sign says otherwise, what is the maximum speed limit on every road except unpaved roads and roads in school, business, or residential areas?
questions.explain: The default speed limit is 55 MPH on all other roads.

questions.prompt: Which set of default speed limits is correct when no speed limit sign is posted?
choices: 35 MPH in residential areas, 25 MPH on unpaved roads and 55 MPH on all other roads
25 MPH in residential areas, 45 MPH on unpaved roads and 65 MPH on all other roads
25 MPH in residential areas, 35 MPH on unpaved roads and 55 MPH on all other roads
15 MPH in residential areas, 35 MPH on unpaved roads and 45 MPH on all other roads
questions.explain: The default limits are 25 MPH in school, business and residential areas, 35 MPH on unpaved roads and 55 MPH on all other roads.

questions.prompt: What does a sign that says SPEED PHOTO ENFORCED mean in a school zone?
choices: You may take photos while you drive
Cameras are used to enforce the speed limit
questions.explain: Some school zones use cameras to check your speed. A sign that says Speed Photo Enforced tells you cameras are in use there.

questions.prompt: Which of these do some school zones have?
choices: Higher speed limits during school hours
questions.explain: Some school zones use automated photo enforcement, and signs that say Speed Photo Enforced tell drivers about it.

questions.prompt: What are the three factors that determine your stopping distance?
choices: Perception time, reaction distance and braking distance
Speed limit, lane width and traffic signs
Following distance, mirrors and blind spots
Engine size, fuel level and tire color
questions.explain: Your stopping distance is made up of perception time, reaction distance and braking distance.

questions.prompt: What is perception time?
choices: The time it takes you to recognize a hazard
The distance your car travels after you brake
The time it takes your brakes to cool
The distance between you and the car ahead
questions.explain: Perception time is the time it takes you to recognize a hazard.

questions.prompt: Which of these affects perception time, reaction distance and braking distance?
questions.explain: Perception time, reaction distance and braking distance are all affected by weather, visibility, and your mental and physical condition.

questions.prompt: Which of these change your ability to stop?
questions.explain: Road conditions, speed, driver alertness and vehicle weight all change your ability to stop.

questions.prompt: What do we call the distance your vehicle travels between the time you recognize a problem and the time you apply the brakes?
questions.explain: Reaction distance is how far your vehicle travels from the time you recognize a problem to the time you apply the brakes.

questions.prompt: What is reaction distance?
choices: The distance your car travels after you apply the brakes
The time it takes you to recognize a hazard
The distance your car travels from recognizing a problem to applying the brakes
The space between your car and the curb
questions.explain: Reaction distance is the distance your car travels from the time you recognize a problem until you apply the brakes.

questions.prompt: What is braking distance?
choices: The distance your car travels after you apply the brakes
The distance your car travels before you apply the brakes
The time it takes you to see a hazard
The distance you should follow behind a truck
questions.explain: Braking distance is the distance your car travels after you apply the brakes.

questions.prompt: Which of these affects your braking distance?
choices: The condition of your brakes and tires
questions.explain: Your speed, the condition of your brakes and tires, and the pavement condition all affect braking distance.

questions.prompt: Which of these will make your braking distance longer?
questions.explain: A higher speed makes your braking distance longer.

questions.prompt: What can wet pavement do?
choices: It can cut your braking distance in half
It can double your braking distance
It can have no effect on your braking distance
It can make antilock brakes stop working
questions.explain: Wet pavement can double your braking distance.

questions.prompt: Compared to dry pavement, how long can your braking distance be on wet pavement?
questions.explain: Wet pavement can double your braking distance, so it can be twice as long.

questions.prompt: It is raining. What should you do to allow for a longer braking distance?
choices: Follow closer so you can see the brake lights
Slow down and leave more space
questions.explain: Wet pavement can double your braking distance, so you should slow down and leave more space.

questions.prompt: What should you do if your vehicle has antilock brakes?
choices: Pump the brakes quickly in a hard stop
Pump the brakes slowly on wet roads
questions.explain: With antilock brakes, you should never pump the brakes.

questions.prompt: What should you do before you drive a vehicle with antilock brakes?
choices: Check the owner's manual and practice braking
questions.explain: Check your owner's manual and practice braking so you understand how antilock brakes work.

questions.prompt: Which statement about antilock brakes is correct?
choices: You should pump them on wet pavement
questions.explain: You should never pump antilock brakes.

questions.prompt: What should you do to create a space cushion around your vehicle?
choices: Stay close to the car ahead
Stay in the middle of your lane
questions.explain: You create a space cushion by staying in the middle of your lane.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a space cushion around your vehicle is correct?
choices: It is needed only on unpaved roads
It gives you room to react and avoid a crash
It is the same as your blind spot
questions.explain: Space around your vehicle gives you distance to react in emergencies and avoid a crash.

questions.prompt: When you drive under 35 MPH on a dry road, what is the shortest following distance you should keep behind the vehicle ahead?
questions.explain: Under 35 MPH, you should stay at least 2 seconds behind the vehicle ahead.

questions.prompt: You are driving 30 MPH on a dry road. What is the safe following distance behind the vehicle ahead?
questions.explain: Under 35 MPH, you should use a following distance of at least 2 seconds.

questions.prompt: What should your following distance be at speeds of 35 to 45 MPH on a dry road?
questions.explain: At 35 to 45 MPH, you should stay at least 3 seconds behind the vehicle ahead.

questions.prompt: You are driving 45 MPH on a dry road. How far behind the vehicle ahead should you be?
questions.explain: From 35 to 45 MPH, you should follow at least 3 seconds behind the vehicle ahead.

questions.prompt: When you drive 46 to 70 MPH on a dry road, what is the shortest following distance you should keep behind the vehicle ahead?
questions.explain: At 46 to 70 MPH, you should stay at least 4 seconds behind the vehicle ahead.

questions.prompt: When do the rules for staying two, three or four seconds behind another car not work?
choices: When you drive on a dry road
questions.explain: The rules for staying two, three or four seconds behind another car do not work when you speed over 70 MPH.

questions.prompt: Which set of following distances is correct for each speed range on a dry road?
choices: 1 second under 35 MPH, 2 seconds at 35 to 45 MPH and 3 seconds at 46 to 70 MPH
3 seconds under 35 MPH, 4 seconds at 35 to 45 MPH and 5 seconds at 46 to 70 MPH
2 seconds under 35 MPH, 3 seconds at 35 to 45 MPH and 4 seconds at 46 to 70 MPH
2 seconds under 35 MPH, 4 seconds at 35 to 45 MPH and 6 seconds at 46 to 70 MPH
questions.explain: Use 2 seconds under 35 MPH, 3 seconds at 35 to 45 MPH and 4 seconds at 46 to 70 MPH.

questions.prompt: To check your following distance, you count the seconds it takes you to reach something. What is it?
choices: A fixed object that the vehicle ahead just passed
questions.explain: Watch the vehicle ahead pass a fixed object. Then count the seconds it takes you to reach that same object.

questions.prompt: You are driving 40 MPH. The car ahead passes a sign. You reach the sign after counting only two seconds. What should you do?
choices: Slow down and increase your following distance
Move closer to the car ahead
questions.explain: If you reach the sign before you count the right number of seconds, you are following too closely, so slow down.

questions.prompt: Which of these can you use as a fixed object when you count your following distance?
questions.explain: You can use any fixed mark, such as an overpass, sign, fence or corner.

questions.prompt: When should you add extra seconds to your following distance?
choices: When your vehicle is in poor condition
questions.explain: Add extra seconds for bad weather, heavy traffic, poor pavement or a vehicle in poor condition.

questions.prompt: What should you do when speed or road conditions change?
questions.explain: Drivers need to change their following distance when speed or road conditions change.

questions.prompt: The road surface is in poor condition. What should your following distance be?
choices: Longer than the usual 2, 3 or 4 seconds
The same as on a dry road
questions.explain: On poor pavement, you should add extra seconds to your following distance.

questions.prompt: Normally, how long is a driver's foot response time?
questions.explain: Foot response time is normally three-quarters of a second.

questions.prompt: About how long is a driver's hand response time?
questions.explain: Hand response time is close to a half second.

questions.prompt: Which of these can delay your perception time?
questions.explain: Being tired, on medication or distracted can delay your perception time.

questions.prompt: When should you increase your following distance?
choices: When you drive behind a large vehicle that blocks your view
When you drive behind a motorcycle or bicycle
questions.explain: You should increase your following distance behind large vehicles, motorcycles and bicycles, and when you exit an expressway.

questions.prompt: Which of these situations calls for a larger following distance?
choices: You are driving on a dry, empty road
The car ahead is far away
questions.explain: You should increase your following distance when someone is tailgating you.

questions.prompt: Why should you increase your following distance behind a large truck?
choices: Large trucks always drive faster than cars
Large trucks never use their brake lights
A large truck blocks your view of the road ahead
The extra space is required only at night
questions.explain: You should increase your following distance behind a large vehicle that blocks your view.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you are being tailgated?
choices: Brake suddenly to warn the driver behind you
Speed up to get away from the driver behind you
Stop in the middle of the road
Move to another lane if you can, or gently tap your brakes and slow down
questions.explain: Do not brake suddenly. Move to another lane if you can, or gently tap your brakes and slow down.

questions.prompt: What is tailgating?
choices: Parking too close to a hydrant
questions.explain: Tailgating is when one driver follows another driver too closely.

questions.prompt: What should you do to help the driver behind you?
choices: Brake hard without giving any warning
Keep a steady speed and tap your brakes before you slow down
Drive in the blind spot of the driver behind you
questions.explain: Keep a safe following distance and a steady speed. Tap your brakes before you slow down or stop.

questions.prompt: Where do expert drivers try to focus their eyes?
choices: On the road 2 to 3 seconds ahead
On the road 5 to 10 seconds ahead
On the road 20 to 30 seconds ahead
On the middle of the road
questions.explain: Expert drivers try to focus their eyes 20 to 30 seconds ahead.

questions.prompt: In the city, looking 20 to 30 seconds ahead means looking about how far?
questions.explain: In the city, 20 to 30 seconds ahead is about one block.

questions.prompt: What should you do when you search the road ahead?
choices: Keep your eyes moving and scan from side to side
Stare at the middle of the road
Watch only the car that is ahead of you
questions.explain: Do not stare at one thing. Keep your eyes moving and scan from side to side.

questions.prompt: What should you do before you enter an intersection?
choices: Look left, then right, then left again
Look right, then left, then right again
questions.explain: Look left, then right, then left again before you enter an intersection.

questions.prompt: Why should you look to the left first at an intersection?
choices: Cars from the right always yield
The signs are on the left
Cars coming from the left will be closer to you
questions.explain: You look left first because cars coming from the left will be closer to you.

questions.prompt: At which places should you look both ways to be sure the way is clear?
questions.explain: Look both ways at any place where cars, people or animals may cross your path.

questions.prompt: What should you do when you reach a place where cars, people or animals may cross your path?
choices: Look both ways to be sure the way is clear
questions.explain: You should look both ways wherever other cars, people or animals may cross your path.

questions.prompt: About how often should you check your rearview mirror?
questions.explain: You should check the traffic behind you often, about every 10 seconds.

questions.prompt: When should you check the traffic behind you?
choices: When you back up or slow down quickly
When you drive down a long, steep hill
questions.explain: You should check behind you when you change lanes, back up, slow down quickly or drive down a long, steep hill.

questions.prompt: What does checking your rearview mirror often do for you?
choices: It makes your following distance longer
It helps you see 20 seconds ahead of your car
It replaces the need to check your blind spot
It alerts you if someone is moving up too quickly or tailgating you
questions.explain: Checking your mirror often alerts you if someone is moving up too quickly or tailgating you.

questions.prompt: Which of these clues warn you that a parked vehicle may pull into your path?
questions.explain: Exhaust smoke, brake or back-up lights, and turned wheels all warn that a vehicle may pull into your path.

questions.prompt: You see exhaust smoke coming from a parked car ahead. What does this mean?
choices: The car may pull into your path
The car is broken down and will never move again
You may pass it at any speed
The driver is signaling you to go
questions.explain: Exhaust smoke is a clue that the car may pull into your path.

questions.prompt: What should you watch for when you drive in rural areas?
choices: Hidden intersections and driveways, curves and hills
questions.explain: In rural areas, you should watch for hidden intersections and driveways, curves, hills and different road conditions.
